lessons.title: Base and Quote Currency: Reading USD/INR the Right Way

children.text: A headline says "Rupee falls 45 paise to 95.95." Your USD/INR chart on the NSE website shows a green candle going up. A friend who trades EUR/USD says the euro is "at 1.16." All three are correct, and all three trip up beginners because they read a currency quote the way they read a share price. Get this lesson wrong and you will buy when you meant to sell. Get it right and every currency number you see for the rest of your life will make sense in two seconds.

body.text: A currency pair always tells you how much of the second currency buys one unit of the first. In USD/INR at 95.50, the dollar is the product and the rupee is the price tag.

children.text: Base and Quote: The Two Halves of Every Pair

markDefs.definition: The first currency in a pair. The quote always tells you the price of exactly one unit of it.
The second currency in a pair. The number in the quote is expressed in this currency.

children.text: Every pair has a
base currency
on the left and a
quote currency

on the right. The number tells you how many units of the quote currency one unit of the base currency costs. Treat the base like a share of Infosys and the quote currency like the rupees you pay for it.

body.latex: 1 \text{ unit of base currency} = \text{Quote} \times 1 \text{ unit of quote currency}
body.caption: USD/INR = 95.50 means 1 US dollar = 95.50 Indian rupees
Reading common pairs (illustrative rates, consistent with USD/INR at 95.50)

body.text: Notice the yen row. One yen is worth well under a rupee, so a per-yen quote would be an awkward 0.6367. Indian exchanges and banks quote JPY/INR per 100 yen instead. Always check the unit before you compare a JPY/INR number with anything else.

children.text: The Direction Trap: Up Means the Rupee Is Weaker

This is the single most common beginner mistake. When USD/INR rises from 95.50 to 95.95, the number went up, but the rupee went down. It now takes more rupees to buy the same dollar. The chart shows what is happening to the base currency, the dollar. The rupee's story is the mirror image.

At a record high vs rupee
At a record low vs dollar

body.title: Which way did it go?
body.question: USD/INR moves from 95.50 at the open to 94.90 at the close. What happened?
options: Nothing, because the rupee has no price in rupees
body.explanation: USD/INR fell, so each dollar now costs fewer rupees. The rupee gained 60 paise against the dollar, and the dollar weakened by the same amount in rupee terms.

body.text: The direction trap costs real money in trading. On NSE or BSE, buying a USD/INR futures contract is a bet that the dollar rises and the rupee falls. If you think the rupee will strengthen, you sell USD/INR. Traders who confuse the two end up positioned exactly opposite to their view.

children.text: Direct and Indirect Quotes

markDefs.definition: A quote showing how much home currency buys one unit of foreign currency. For an Indian, USD/INR at 95.50 is a direct quote.
A quote showing how much foreign currency one unit of home currency buys. For an Indian, INR/USD at 0.010471 is an indirect quote.

children.text: India uses a
direct quote
: rupees per unit of foreign currency. That is intuitive for a shopper, because it works like a price tag. The flip side is the
indirect quote
: how many dollars one rupee buys. You get it by dividing 1 by the direct quote.

body.caption: One rupee buys about 0.010471 dollars, or roughly 1.05 US cents

body.title: The same market, two ways of writing it

columns.label: Direct quote (how India quotes)
points: Number rises when the rupee weakens
Used by RBI, FBIL, NSE, BSE and Indian banks

columns.label: Indirect quote (the inverse)
points: Number falls when the rupee weakens
Useful for measuring the rupee's own value

body.title: What One Rupee Buys: US Cents per Rupee (year-end, approx.)

children.text: This is the same history as the rising USD/INR chart from Chapter 1, flipped upside down. When the rupee's own value is plotted, the decline is obvious: one rupee bought about 1.37 US cents at the end of 2020 and only about 1.05 cents in September 2026.
Why the Dollar's Gain Is Not the Rupee's Loss, in Percent

The same move gives two different percentages because each is measured from a different starting point. When someone says "the rupee fell 6%," check whether they mean the rise in USD/INR or the drop in the rupee's own value. For small daily moves the gap is tiny. For moves over a year or more, it matters.

content.caption: Measured with USD/INR, the direct quote
Measured with INR/USD, the indirect quote

children.text: The two are linked: (1 + 6.11%) × (1 minus 5.76%) = 1.0611 × 0.9424 ≈ 1. A currency that rises by x% against another is matched by a fall of x ÷ (1 + x) in the other direction, which is always a slightly smaller number.

body.title: How much did the rupee lose?
body.prompt: At the end of 2022, USD/INR was about 82.70. In September 2026 it was about 95.50. By what percentage did the rupee lose value against the dollar? Enter a positive number rounded to two decimals.
body.explanation: Rupee change = 82.70 ÷ 95.50 minus 1 = 0.8660 minus 1 = minus 13.40%. The dollar's gain over the same period was 95.50 ÷ 82.70 minus 1 = 15.48%. Same move, two different percentages.

children.text: Which Currency Goes First? Market Conventions

You rarely get to choose how a pair is written. Global dealers follow a fixed order of precedence so that everyone quotes the same way: euro first, then the British pound, then the Australian and New Zealand dollars, then the US dollar, then almost everything else. That is why it is EUR/USD and GBP/USD, but USD/JPY and USD/INR. The rupee sits below the dollar, the euro and the pound, so in all of India's main pairs, the rupee is the quote currency.

body.title: Name the base
body.textWithBlank: In the pair GBP/USD quoted at 1.3400, the base currency is the ___.
body.explanation: The base is always on the left. GBP/USD at 1.3400 means £1 costs $1.34.

children.text: Cross Rates: Building EUR/INR From Two Pairs

markDefs.definition: An exchange rate between two currencies calculated through a third, usually the US dollar.

children.text: Most rupee trading is against the dollar, so the rupee's price against the euro or the pound is usually worked out through the dollar. This is called a
cross rate
. The trick is to line up the currencies so the dollar cancels out.

body.caption: Euros to dollars, then dollars to rupees. The dollar cancels out.

children.text: When the dollar sits on the left of both pairs, you divide instead. JPY/INR = USD/INR ÷ USD/JPY = 95.50 ÷ 150.00 = 0.6367 per yen, which is ₹63.67 per 100 yen. A quick sanity check: the answer should make sense in plain words. A euro is worth more than a dollar, so EUR/INR must be above USD/INR. A yen is worth much less than a rupee, so JPY/INR per yen must be below 1.

body.title: Price a pound
body.prompt: GBP/USD is 1.3400 and USD/INR is 95.50. What is GBP/INR? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: GBP/INR = GBP/USD × USD/INR = 1.3400 × 95.50 = 127.97. Pounds to dollars, then dollars to rupees, with the dollar cancelling out.

body.label: UAE dirham peg to the US dollar
body.context: The UAE central bank has held this fixed rate since 1997. Because the dirham is pegged, AED/INR moves almost exactly in line with USD/INR, which is why Gulf remittances rise in rupee terms whenever the rupee weakens against the dollar.

body.title: The Dubai remittance
body.scenario: Faisal works in Dubai and sends AED 5,000 home to his parents in Kozhikode every month. His exchange app shows USD/AED at 3.6725 and USD/INR at 95.50. Last year, when USD/INR was 85.60, the same AED 5,000 was worth less. His mother asks why the money "went up" when Faisal's salary did not change.
body.prompt: Work out AED/INR today, how many rupees AED 5,000 is worth now versus last year, and explain the increase to his mother in one or two sentences. Ignore app fees.
body.modelAnswer:
1. The dollar is on the left of both pairs, so divide: AED/INR = USD/INR ÷ USD/AED = 95.50 ÷ 3.6725 = 26.00 rupees per dirham (26.0041 unrounded).
2. Today: AED 5,000 × 26.0041 = about ₹1,30,020.
3. Last year: AED/INR = 85.60 ÷ 3.6725 = 23.3084, so AED 5,000 = about ₹1,16,542.
4. The increase is about ₹13,478, even though Faisal sent the same number of dirhams.
5. Explanation for his mother: the dirham is tied to the dollar, and the rupee has become weaker against the dollar, so each dirham now buys more rupees. The salary did not rise. The rupee fell.

cards.definition: The first currency in a pair. The quote shows the price of one unit of it.
The second currency in a pair. The number is expressed in this currency.
Home currency per unit of foreign currency. USD/INR at 95.50 is a direct quote for Indians.
Foreign currency per unit of home currency. INR/USD at 0.010471 is its inverse.
A rate between two currencies calculated through a third, usually the US dollar, such as EUR/INR from EUR/USD and USD/INR.
The rupee losing value, shown as USD/INR rising.

points: In any pair, the number is the price of one unit of the base currency, expressed in the quote currency.
USD/INR rising means the dollar is stronger and the rupee is weaker. Buying USD/INR is a bet against the rupee.
India uses direct quotes. The inverse, INR/USD, shows what one rupee buys.
A dollar gain and the matching rupee loss are different percentages: 90.00 to 95.50 is +6.11% for the dollar and -5.76% for the rupee.
Global convention puts EUR, GBP, AUD and NZD before USD, and USD before the rupee, so the rupee is always the quote currency in its main pairs.
Cross rates like EUR/INR and AED/INR are built through the dollar: multiply when the dollar cancels across the pairs, divide when the dollar is the base in both.
JPY/INR is quoted per 100 yen in India, so always check the unit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Exchange rates other than the historical USD/INR levels are illustrative and chosen for easy calculation. Check live rates before making any transaction.
